detectors.rationale: A plain <input id="cardnumber"> lets merchant JavaScript read the raw PAN and CVV straight off the DOM via .value, pulling the entire page into full PCI-DSS card-data scope; the safe idiom mounts a Stripe CardNumberElement, which renders inside a Stripe-controlled iframe so the merchant page never sees or touches the raw PAN.

Writing raw PAN/CVV into localStorage (and into an analytics event) persists prohibited cardholder data on the client where any XSS or compromised script can read it long after the checkout session ends; the safe idiom persists only the tokenized paymentMethod id returned by Stripe, never the raw card fields.

POSTing the raw pan/cvv/exp fields straight to a first-party /api/pay endpoint routes cardholder data through the merchant's own server and logs, expanding PCI-DSS scope to the whole backend; the safe idiom calls stripe.createToken(cardElement) first and POSTs only the resulting single-use token, so raw card data never leaves the browser's Stripe context.

Loading a third-party script on the payment page with no Subresource Integrity hash means a compromised CDN can silently swap in a script that skims card fields, with nothing to detect the tampering (PCI-DSS 6.4.3); the safe idiom adds an integrity="sha256-..." attribute (plus crossorigin) so a modified payload fails to execute.

Building the card-number, expiry, and CVC fields as plain React <input> elements gives the merchant's own component tree direct DOM access to every keystroke of cardholder data with no hosted-field/iframe sandbox in between; the safe idiom renders a single <PaymentElement />, which Stripe mounts inside its own sandboxed iframes so none of the raw fields ever enter merchant-controlled DOM.
